title: Doubts vanish
hook: after awakening he reviews dependent origination, and doubts vanish like mist
tomorrow: In the seen, only the seen

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Udana, a book of words breathed out, and your line, spoken from joy. Did something make you breathe out? Today, the very first udana, from the first week after the awakening. Day six hundred twelve.

The book doesn't start with a crowd or a sermon. It starts under a tree. The Buddha has just awakened, at Uruvela, on the bank of the Neranjara river, at the foot of the bodhi tree. And for seven days, the text says, he sits there in one cross-legged posture, feeling the happiness of release. No teaching yet. No students. Just a man sitting by a river for a week. At the end of those seven days, he does something very specific with his mind, through the watches of the night. Today: doubts vanish.
screen: `UNDER THE TREE, BY THE RIVER.` → `SEVEN DAYS IN ONE POSTURE.` → `THEN, THREE WATCHES OF THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the first watch of the night, he attends to dependent origination in forward order: when this is, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises. Ignorance gives rise to formations, formations to consciousness, and so on, link by link, to the whole mass of suffering. And the verse comes: when things become clear to the one who meditates with ardor, his doubts all vanish, because he understands a thing together with its cause. The next udana: the same, in reverse. When this is not, that does not come to be; with the ending of this, that ends. Doubts vanish, because he understands the ending of causes. The third: both directions together. And this time the verse adds an image: he stands, scattering Mara's army, like the sun lighting up the sky. Notice how doubt goes in this story. Not by being argued with. Not by being pushed down. It goes because something is seen: this comes from that. Elsewhere the early texts list doubt among the hindrances: the wobbling that can't decide. What ends it isn't certainty about everything. It's seeing one cause clearly. Mist doesn't need to be fought. The sun comes up, and it's gone.
screen: `FORWARD: THIS ARISES FROM THAT.` · `BACKWARD: THIS ENDS WITH THAT.` · `BOTH, AND MARA'S ARMY SCATTERS.` · `SEEING A CAUSE ENDS DOUBT.` · then, large: `DOUBTS VANISH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace one cause. Sit and settle. Pick one feeling that's here right now: a bit of tiredness, worry, a flicker of irritation. Ask, gently, where did this come from? Maybe a short night. Maybe a message you read. Follow it one link back, then one more if it's there. Don't analyze too hard. Just see: this came from that. Notice whether the feeling changes when its cause is seen. The bell holds the time.
Doubts vanish. The first three udanas: when the Buddha sees how each thing arises from its cause, his doubts vanish, and in the third verse he shines like the sun lighting up the sky. Today's word.
Your line: doubts vanish. Today, when you can't decide something, look for one cause underneath it, and see if the fog thins. Day six hundred twelve.

screen: `DAY 612 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IN THE SEEN, ONLY THE SEEN.`

howItsDone: Dependent origination is taught across Buddhist schools, and some Theravada chanting books set out its links in forward and reverse order, as in the opening of the Udana.

pairs: a hindrance: wobbling that can't decide

myth: right after awakening, the Buddha began teaching at once
the Udana says he sat for seven days in one posture, feeling the happiness of release.
in the verse, doubts vanish because a thing is understood with its cause
the first udana ties the end of doubt to seeing causes.
the third udana compares him to the sun lighting up the sky
he stands scattering Mara's army, like the sun in the sky.

fork.setup: you've just awakened, sitting by a river. a week has passed in stillness. what does the Buddha do, in the Udana's first story?
options: walk straight to the nearest town to teach.
attend to how each thing arises from its cause, through the night.
fork.reveal: he reviews dependent origination, forward, then back, then both. after the first two, the verse says his doubts vanish; after the third, he stands like the sun lighting up the sky.

original.note: Pali kankha: doubt, the wavering that can't decide. in Udana 1.1 the doubts (kankha) all vanish.

trapdoor: what you thought: doubt goes away when you believe hard enough.
what it means: in the first udanas, doubt vanishes when a thing is seen together with its cause.
what a scholar hears: Udana 1.1–1.3 review paticcasamuppada forward (anuloma), reverse (patiloma) and both, a sequence also found at the opening of the Vinaya's Mahavagga.

notes: Udana 1.1–1.3 paraphrased. Confirm that the three suttas assign forward, reverse and both orders to the first, middle and last watches.
The outline's 'like mist' is not in the text; the script uses mist as its own image and keeps the text's sun simile in the third verse. Confirm.

Reviewer: the hook originally said 'three nights in a row'. The Udana repeats the seven-day frame in each of 1.1–1.3, while the Vinaya Mahavagga places all three watches in one night; whether it is one night or three is read differently, so the hook now says 'through the watches of the night'.

Reviewer: the third verse speaks of Mara's army and the sun, not of doubts vanishing; the fork reveal and the word segment were adjusted so they no longer say every verse ends doubt, and the word segment no longer attributes the mist image to the text.

Editor review (2026-10-01): Udana 1.1 itself names the bodhi tree, so 'the tree we now call' was dropped; the count 'five hindrances' is outside today's cited text and was softened in the teach and match game; howItsDone's 'every Buddhist tradition' and 'many Theravada monasteries' were softened.
